lesson.title: The Formula Behind Every Derivative
lesson.summary: States the limit definition of the derivative in both its h-form and x-form, then checks a single derivative two independent ways to confirm they must agree.
lesson.body:
With the idea of the derivative established as a limit that captures both slope and instantaneous rate, it is time to write down its definition in the precise form used throughout calculus. The derivative of a function f at a point x = a is f prime of a equals the limit as h approaches 0 of the quotient [f(a + h) minus f(a)] divided by h, whenever that limit exists. This quotient is often called the difference quotient, since its numerator is a difference of function values and it is divided by the change in input, h.

There is a second, equivalent way to write the same limit, which some problems make easier to work with. Instead of writing the second point as a + h, write it simply as x, and let x approach a directly: f prime of a equals the limit as x approaches a of [f(x) minus f(a)] divided by (x minus a). Both versions describe the same rotating secant line and produce the same number; the first tracks a small step h from a, and the second tracks a nearby point x heading toward a. Which one to use is a matter of convenience for the algebra in front of you.

Try both forms on f(x) = x cubed at a = 2. Using the h form: f prime of 2 equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [(2 + h) cubed minus 2 cubed] divided by h. Expanding (2 + h) cubed gives 8 plus 12h plus 6h squared plus h cubed. Subtracting 8 leaves 12h plus 6h squared plus h cubed, which factors as h times (12 plus 6h plus h squared). Dividing by h gives 12 plus 6h plus h squared, and letting h approach 0 leaves 12. So f prime of 2 equals 12.

Now the x form, as a check: f prime of 2 equals the limit as x approaches 2 of (x cubed minus 8) divided by (x minus 2). The numerator factors using the difference of cubes pattern: x cubed minus 8 equals (x minus 2) times (x squared plus 2x plus 4). The factor (x minus 2) cancels with the denominator, leaving x squared plus 2x plus 4, valid for all x near 2 except exactly at 2. Substituting x = 2 directly now works fine: 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 12. Both routes agree exactly: f prime of 2 equals 12.

Both forms reappear constantly. The h form was already used to find the tangent slope of f(x) = x squared at x = 3, where [(3 + h) squared minus 9] divided by h simplified to 6 + h before the limit gave 6. The x form is especially convenient whenever the numerator factors cleanly against (x minus a), as it just did for x cubed minus 8. Neither form is more correct than the other, they are the same statement written with different bookkeeping, and fluent use of the limit definition means being able to switch between them whenever one makes the surrounding algebra shorter.

This agreement is not a coincidence, it is guaranteed by the algebra of substitution, and it is a good habit to check a derivative computation using whichever form makes the factoring cleanest. Polynomials often factor nicely in the x minus a form, while expansion is usually easier in the h form. Either way, the limit definition is the one rule underneath every derivative rule you will later learn as a shortcut, and this flexibility becomes especially valuable once the functions being differentiated grow more complicated than simple polynomials.
